The Blue-legged mantella (Mantella expectata) is a small, brightly colored dendrobatid frog endemic to the arid, rocky outcrops of south-central Madagascar. Adult females in this species attain a larger ultimate snout-vent length of 3 centimeters [Li = 3 centimeters] when fully grown, whereas males are more diminutive, reaching an ultimate SVL of 2.7 centimeters [Li = 2.7 centimeters]. This noticeable sexual size dimorphism is characteristic of many Mantella species and is thought to relate to the demands of egg production in females. Newly metamorphosed froglets emerge from their aquatic larval phase at a body length of 1.6 centimeters , a stage at which they transition to a completely terrestrial existence. Reflecting their specialized microhabitat, these frogs inhabit sun-drenched granite and quartzite shelves, where their vivid blue and yellow legs serve as an aposematic signal against the pale stone, advertising the presence of alkaloid toxins sequestered from their arthropod diet.

Under controlled laboratory conditions, the developmental trajectory from oviposition to metamorphosis in Mantella expectata is strongly mediated by temperature. When eggs are incubated and larvae are reared at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the time from birth to metamorphosis is approximately 180 days . This lengthy larval period is considerably longer than the 20 to 32 days typically cited for many lowland tropical anurans, likely reflecting the slower developmental pace required for the biosynthesis of cutaneous alkaloids from dietary precursors during the tadpole stage. The fertilized eggs, which are deposited in small, gelatinous clutches among moist leaf litter or in shallow rock depressions, are initially quite small. Each newly hatched tadpole carries a wet weight of only 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] at birth, a minuscule mass that necessitates a rapid onset of filter-feeding to sustain subsequent growth through the early larval instars.

The attainment of reproductive maturity in male Blue-legged mantellas is marked by a distinct shift in body size, with published accounts documenting two slightly different size thresholds for the completion of puberty. Some field-based studies have indicated that males reach sexual maturity at a snout-vent length of 2.8 centimeters [Lp = 2.8 centimeters], a size that may reflect the attainment of full spermatogenic activity in individuals from more productive habitats. Conversely, other reports suggest that puberty can be achieved at a slightly smaller body length of 2.5 centimeters [Lp = 2.5 centimeters], perhaps representing a more conservative threshold under conditions of resource limitation or high population density. These figures, while differing numerically, both highlight a general pattern in which males are capable of reproductive activity at sizes substantially smaller than the species' maximum, thereby maximizing their opportunities to compete for mates in a lek-like breeding system. Females, in contrast, delay their first reproduction until they have reached a larger body size to support the energetic burden of oogenesis.

The maximum reproductive output of Mantella expectata has been estimated based on comparative scaling relationships with the well-studied water frog Pelophylax esculentus. When maintained at an ambient temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], an individual female can produce approximately 10 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 10 eggs per clutch] and can deposit about 21 clutches per year [F_R_i = about 21 clutches per year], which together yield an annual fecundity of roughly 210 eggs per 365-day year [Ri = roughly 210 eggs per 365-day year]. This comparatively modest reproductive output is consistent with the species' life-history strategy as an income breeder, where reproductive effort is tightly coupled with periods of high prey abundance during the austral summer rains. Regarding ultimate body mass, the wet weight of a fully grown adult female has been modeled from length-weight allometry to be 2.755 grams [Wwi = 2.755 grams], a substantial investment in soma that underpins the production of large, yolk-rich eggs. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult males is correspondingly lower, calculated at 2.01 grams [Wwi = 2.01 grams], reflecting their smaller skeletal frame.

Longevity data for wild populations of Mantella expectata remain scarce, but captive-rearing programs and mark-recapture efforts have provided a solid baseline for maximum lifespan. The oldest documented individuals reach an age of approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years] when maintained at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], though this figure may be a conservative estimate for wild frogs experiencing less predictable thermal regimes. In comparison to many other small-bodied anurans, which rarely exceed two years in nature, this life span suggests a relatively slow life-history pace characterized by deferred reproduction and extended breeding tenure. The species' reliance on aposematism likely reduces extrinsic mortality from predation, thereby allowing the evolution of a longer adult phase. In the wild, survivorship is further modulated by the severe dry-season conditions of their xeric habitat, where frogs must aestivate in rock crevices, a behavior that imposes a metabolic bottleneck that may limit both growth rate and ultimate size.
